title: JavaScript from Zero

mentor.name: LOOP-7
mentor.character: Shows you exactly what the browser sees and never pretends the console is a mystery.

summary: Start from a blank script tag and finish writing an interactive web page that fetches real data. On the way you learn variables, functions, arrays, objects, the DOM, events, fetch and async/await, one mission at a time.

lessons.title: Your first variable with let
lessons.goal: Declare a variable with let and assign a string value to it.
lessons.theory:
JavaScript runs in every browser. You write code in a `<script>` tag or a `.js` file and the browser runs it top to bottom.

The most common way to create a variable is `let`:

```javascript
let message = "hello";
console.log(message);
```

`let` declares a new name. The `=` stores a value in it. `console.log` is JavaScript's version of print, it sends output to the browser console.

Strings are text between single or double quotes. Both work. The semicolon at the end of a line is optional in modern JavaScript, but including it is a good habit.
lessons.task: Declare a variable called `greeting` and assign the string `"Hello, world!"` to it. Do not print anything yet.
lessons.solution: let greeting = "Hello, world!";
lessons.hint: Start with `let`, then the name, then `=`, then the string in quotes.

lessons.title: const for values that never change
lessons.goal: Use const to store a value that should not be reassigned.
lessons.theory:
`const` is like `let` but the name can never be pointed at a different value after the first assignment. If you try, JavaScript throws a `TypeError`.

```javascript
const PI = 3.14159;
```

Using `const` is the right default. Switch to `let` only when you know the value will need to change. This way anyone reading the code knows at a glance that a `const` name will hold the same value from that line on.

`var` is the old way and has confusing scoping rules. Do not use it in new code.
lessons.task: Declare a constant called `SITE_NAME` and assign the string `"Zerack Academy"` to it.
lessons.solution: const SITE_NAME = "Zerack Academy";
lessons.hint: Replace `let` with `const` and give it the right name and value.

lessons.title: Numbers and arithmetic
lessons.goal: Store two numbers and compute their product.
lessons.task: Declare `width` as `8`, `height` as `5`, and `area` as their product. No output needed.
lessons.hint: Three `let` declarations. The third one multiplies the first two with `*`.

lessons.title: Booleans: true and false
lessons.goal: Declare a boolean variable and understand what it represents.
lessons.theory:
A **boolean** holds one of two values: `true` or `false`. No quotes.

```javascript
let isOnline = true;
let hasErrors = false;
```

Booleans are the result of comparisons and are used to make decisions. `===` checks whether two values are equal. `!==` checks whether they differ. You will use them constantly in `if` statements.

Capitalization matters: `True` or `TRUE` are not booleans, they are undefined names.
lessons.task: Declare a variable `loggedIn` set to `true` and a variable `isAdmin` set to `false`.
lessons.solution:
let loggedIn = true;
let isAdmin = false;
lessons.hint: Two lines, each starting with `let`. Booleans are lowercase and have no quotes.

lessons.title: Template literals
lessons.goal: Build a sentence that includes variable values using template literals.
lessons.task: Given `let city = "Madrid"` and `let temp = 22`, log a template literal that produces the text `Madrid is 22 degrees`.
lessons.hint: Use backticks (not quotes) for the string, and wrap each variable in `${}`.

lessons.title: Comparison operators
lessons.goal: Use === and !== to compare two values and store the result.
lessons.theory:
Comparison operators return `true` or `false`:

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `===` | strictly equal (same value and type) |
| `!==` | strictly not equal |
| `>` | greater than |
| `<` | less than |
| `>=` | greater than or equal |
| `<=` | less than or equal |

Always prefer `===` over `==`. The double-equals `==` does type coercion and gives surprising results: `0 == false` is `true`, `0 === false` is `false`.
lessons.task: Declare `let x = 10`. Then declare `let isPositive` and set it to the result of `x > 0`. Declare `let isTen` and set it to the result of `x === 10`.
lessons.hint: The right side of each assignment is just the comparison expression, no `if` needed.

lessons.title: Logical operators
lessons.goal: Combine conditions with && and ||.
lessons.task: Given `let hour = 14` and `let isWeekday = true`, declare `let officeOpen` set to `true` when `hour` is between 9 and 18 (inclusive) AND `isWeekday` is `true`.
lessons.hint: Use `&&` to join all three conditions into one expression.

lessons.title: The typeof operator
lessons.goal: Use typeof to find out what type a value has.
lessons.theory:
`typeof` is a unary operator that returns a string naming the type:

```javascript
console.log(typeof 42);        // "number"
console.log(typeof "hello");   // "string"
console.log(typeof true);      // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined); // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);      // "object"  (historical quirk)
```

Note the historical bug: `typeof null` returns `"object"`, not `"null"`. Use `=== null` to test for null specifically.
lessons.task: What does `typeof "hello"` return?
lessons.solution: string
lessons.hint: The result is a lowercase string in double quotes.

why: Correct: typeof always returns a lowercase string, and strings are identified as "string".
That is not a valid typeof result in JavaScript.
That is Python's name for strings, not JavaScript's.
object is returned for objects and null, not for plain strings.
check.explain: typeof "hello" returns the string "string" in JavaScript.

lessons.title: Arithmetic shorthand operators
lessons.goal: Update a variable in place using +=, -= and *=.
lessons.theory:
Shorthand assignment operators combine arithmetic and assignment:

```javascript
let score = 10;
score += 5;   // score = score + 5  →  15
score -= 3;   // score = score - 3  →  12
score *= 2;   // score = score * 2  →  24
score /= 4;   // score = score / 4  →  6
```

There is also `++` (add 1) and `--` (subtract 1), though `+= 1` is clearer about intent.

These are purely shorthand. `x += 3` is completely identical to `x = x + 3`.
lessons.task: Start with `let points = 100`. Subtract 20 using `-=`, then multiply by 2 using `*=`. No output needed.
lessons.hint: Two lines after the declaration, each using a shorthand operator.

lessons.title: The ternary operator
lessons.goal: Write a compact conditional expression with the ternary operator.
lessons.theory:
The **ternary operator** is a one-line `if/else` that produces a value:

```javascript
condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
```

Example:

```javascript
let age = 20;
let label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";
console.log(label); // "adult"
```

Use it when both branches produce a simple value and the whole expression fits on one line. For anything more complex, a regular `if/else` reads better.
lessons.task: Given `let score = 75`, declare `let result` using a ternary: if `score >= 60` set it to `"pass"`, otherwise `"fail"`.
lessons.solution:
let score = 75;
let result = score >= 60 ? "pass" : "fail";
lessons.hint: The ternary goes on the right of the `=`. Question mark separates condition from true-branch, colon separates the two branches.

lessons.title: if and else
lessons.goal: Write an if/else block that takes one of two paths.
lessons.task: Given `let battery = 15`, log `"low battery"` if `battery < 20`, otherwise log `"battery ok"`.
lessons.hint: The condition goes in parentheses after `if`. Both branches need curly braces.

lessons.title: else if for multiple branches
lessons.goal: Chain else if to handle more than two cases.
lessons.task: Given `let speed = 85`, log `"too fast"` if speed > 120, `"fast"` if speed > 90, `"normal"` otherwise.
lessons.hint: Three branches: `if`, `else if`, and `else`. The conditions go in order from most restrictive to least.

lessons.title: switch for exact values
lessons.goal: Use a switch statement to branch on a specific set of known values.
lessons.task: Given `let color = "red"`, use a switch to log `"stop"` for `"red"`, `"go"` for `"green"`, and `"caution"` for any other value.
lessons.hint: Three sections: a `case "red"`, a `case "green"`, and a `default`. Each case ends with `break`.

lessons.title: Truthy and falsy values
lessons.goal: Understand which values JavaScript treats as false in a boolean context.
lessons.theory:
JavaScript converts any value to boolean when it is used as a condition. The **falsy** values, those that act like `false`, are exactly:

- `false`
- `0`
- `""` (empty string)
- `null`
- `undefined`
- `NaN`

Everything else is **truthy**, including `"0"`, `[]`, and `{}`.

This means `if (username)` is a short way to check that `username` is neither empty nor null nor undefined. Be careful: it also rejects `0` and `false`, which may or may not be what you want.
lessons.task: Which value is falsy in JavaScript?
lessons.hint: An empty string has no characters, so JavaScript treats it as nothing.

why: Correct: an empty string is one of the six falsy values in JavaScript.
The string "0" is a non-empty string, so it is truthy.
An empty array is an object, and objects are always truthy in JavaScript.
An empty object is also truthy, even with no properties.
check.explain: The six falsy values are false, 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else including "0", [], and {} is truthy.

lessons.title: Nullish coalescing ??
lessons.goal: Use ?? to provide a fallback only when a value is null or undefined.
lessons.task: Given `let userAge = null`, declare `let age` using `??` so it falls back to `18` when `userAge` is null.
lessons.solution:
let userAge = null;
let age = userAge ?? 18;
lessons.hint: Use the `??` operator with `userAge` on the left and `18` on the right.

lessons.title: The for loop
lessons.goal: Use a for loop to repeat a block a fixed number of times.
lessons.task: Write a for loop that logs the numbers 1 through 5, one per line.
lessons.hint: Start `i` at 1, check `i <= 5`, and increment with `i++`.

lessons.title: The while loop
lessons.goal: Use a while loop when the number of iterations is not known up front.
lessons.task: Start with `let n = 1`. Write a while loop that doubles `n` each iteration and stops (does not log the last value) once `n` reaches or exceeds 100. Log `n` at the start of each iteration.
lessons.hint: The condition is `n < 100`. Inside the loop: log first, then `n *= 2`.

lessons.title: for...of over arrays
lessons.goal: Iterate over an array's values with for...of.
lessons.task: Given `const colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]`, write a for...of loop that logs each color.
lessons.hint: The loop variable receives one color per iteration. Use `const` for it.

lessons.title: break and continue
lessons.goal: Use break to exit a loop early and continue to skip an iteration.
lessons.task: Write a for loop from 1 to 10 that logs only odd numbers (skip evens with `continue`) and stops after logging 7 (use `break` after logging 7).
lessons.hint: Use `i % 2 === 0` to detect even numbers. Place the `break` after the log so 7 is still printed.

lessons.title: Function declarations
lessons.goal: Declare a function with parameters and call it.
lessons.theory:
A **function** is a reusable block of code with a name:

```javascript
function greet(name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
}
greet("Ana");  // Hello, Ana!
greet("Leo");  // Hello, Leo!
```

- `function` is the keyword.
- `greet` is the name.
- `name` is a **parameter**: a placeholder filled in when the function is called.
- The value passed when calling is an **argument**.

A function declaration is **hoisted**: you can call it before the line where it is defined.
lessons.task: Declare a function called `square` that takes a number parameter `n` and logs `n * n`. Then call it with the argument `7`.
lessons.hint: Declare first with `function square(n)`, body logs `n * n`, then call `square(7)` below.

lessons.title: return values
lessons.goal: Use return to send a value back from a function.
lessons.task: Write a function `multiply(a, b)` that returns `a * b`. Then declare `let result` equal to `multiply(6, 7)` and log it.
lessons.hint: The function uses `return`, not `console.log`. You log the result outside after calling the function.

lessons.title: Function expressions and arrow functions
lessons.goal: Write a function as a variable using an arrow function.
lessons.task: Declare a const arrow function `cube` that takes `n` and returns `n ** 3`. Log `cube(4)`.
lessons.solution:
const cube = (n) => n ** 3;
console.log(cube(4));
lessons.hint: Use `const cube = (n) => n ** 3;` then log the result of calling it.

lessons.title: Default parameters
lessons.goal: Give a function parameter a default value used when no argument is passed.
lessons.task: Write a function `power(base, exp = 2)` that returns `base ** exp`. Log `power(3)` and `power(3, 3)`.
lessons.hint: The default goes in the parameter list: `exp = 2`. Two separate log calls below the function.

lessons.title: Scope: where a name lives
lessons.goal: Understand that let and const are block-scoped.
lessons.task: Where is a variable declared with `let` inside an `if` block accessible?
lessons.solution: Only inside that if block
lessons.hint: Think about which curly braces enclose the declaration.

options: Only inside the if block where it was declared
Anywhere in the function that contains the if
Only on the exact line where it is declared
why: Correct: let is block-scoped, so it only exists within the {} of the block where it was declared.
That would be true for var, but let is more restricted than that.
Global scope only applies to variables declared outside any function or block.
A variable is accessible from its declaration to the end of its enclosing block, not just that one line.
check.explain: let and const are block-scoped: they live from their declaration to the closing } of the block they are in.

lessons.title: Creating and indexing arrays
lessons.goal: Create an array and read elements by index.
lessons.theory:
An **array** is an ordered list of values:

```javascript
const scores = [95, 82, 78, 91];
console.log(scores[0]); // 95  (first element)
console.log(scores[3]); // 91  (fourth element)
console.log(scores.length); // 4
```

Indexes start at `0`. The last element is at index `length - 1`. Accessing an index that does not exist returns `undefined`, not an error.

Arrays can hold any mix of types, though in practice each array usually holds one type.
lessons.task: Declare `const planets = ["Mercury", "Venus", "Earth", "Mars"]`. Log the first element and the length of the array.
lessons.hint: Access the first element with index 0. The length is a property, not a method, so no parentheses.

lessons.title: push, pop, shift, unshift
lessons.goal: Add and remove elements at both ends of an array.
lessons.theory:
Four methods modify an array's length:

```javascript
const list = [1, 2, 3];
list.push(4);      // add to end    → [1, 2, 3, 4]
list.pop();        // remove from end → [1, 2, 3]
list.unshift(0);   // add to start  → [0, 1, 2, 3]
list.shift();      // remove from start → [1, 2, 3]
```

`push` and `unshift` return the new length. `pop` and `shift` return the removed element.

All four mutate the array in place; they do not create a copy.
lessons.task: Given `const queue = ["a", "b", "c"]`, add `"d"` to the end with `push`, then remove the first element with `shift`. Log the array after both operations.
lessons.hint: `push` and `shift` are called as `queue.push(...)` and `queue.shift()`. Log the whole array at the end.

lessons.title: map: transform every element
lessons.goal: Use map to create a new array by applying a function to each element.
lessons.theory:
`map` calls a callback function for every element and returns a **new array** of the results. It never changes the original:

```javascript
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const doubled = numbers.map(n => n * 2);
console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6, 8]
```

The callback receives the element as its first argument. You can also receive the index as a second argument if you need it.

Because `map` returns an array, you can chain it with other array methods.
lessons.task: Given `const temps = [0, 20, 37, 100]`, create a `const fahrenheit` array using `map` that converts each value with the formula `(c * 9/5) + 32`. Log `fahrenheit`.
lessons.hint: Use an arrow function inside `.map()`. The formula for each element goes in the arrow body.

lessons.title: filter: keep matching elements
lessons.goal: Use filter to create a new array with only the elements that pass a test.
lessons.task: Given `const words = ["cat", "elephant", "ox", "rhinoceros", "dog"]`, use `filter` to create `const longWords` containing only words with more than 4 characters. Log `longWords`.
lessons.hint: Each word has a `.length` property. The callback should return `true` when that length is greater than 4.

lessons.title: reduce: collapse an array to one value
lessons.goal: Use reduce to compute a single value from an array.
lessons.theory:
`reduce` processes each element and accumulates a running result:

```javascript
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
const sum = numbers.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
console.log(sum); // 15
```

The callback takes two arguments: `acc` (the accumulated value so far) and `n` (the current element). The second argument to `reduce` is the **initial value** of the accumulator. Always provide it explicitly.

You can reduce to numbers, strings, objects or arrays.
lessons.task: Given `const prices = [9.99, 4.50, 12.00, 7.25]`, use `reduce` to compute the `total` of all prices. Log `total`.
lessons.hint: The initial value (second argument to reduce) should be `0`. The callback adds each price to the accumulator.

lessons.title: Creating and reading objects
lessons.goal: Create an object literal and read its properties with dot notation.
lessons.theory:
An **object** is a collection of key-value pairs called **properties**:

```javascript
const user = {
  name: "Ana",
  age: 28,
  active: true
};
console.log(user.name);   // "Ana"
console.log(user.age);    // 28
```

Dot notation accesses a property by name. Bracket notation `user["name"]` also works and is needed when the key is stored in a variable.

Objects group related data together. You will use them constantly in real JavaScript.
lessons.task: Create `const book` with properties `title` set to `"Dune"`, `author` set to `"Frank Herbert"`, and `pages` set to `896`. Log `book.title` and `book.pages`.
lessons.hint: Inside the `{}`, each property is `key: value` separated by commas.

lessons.title: Adding and updating properties
lessons.goal: Add a new property and change an existing one after creation.
lessons.task: Given `const person = { name: "Leo", age: 25 }`, change `age` to `26` and add a property `city` set to `"Barcelona"`. Log `person`.
lessons.hint: Two lines after the declaration: one updates `.age`, one adds `.city`. Then log the whole object.

lessons.title: Object destructuring
lessons.goal: Extract several properties into variables with destructuring syntax.
lessons.theory:
**Destructuring** pulls properties out of an object into named variables in one step:

```javascript
const user = { name: "Ana", age: 28, city: "Lima" };
const { name, age } = user;
console.log(name); // "Ana"
console.log(age);  // 28
```

You can rename while destructuring:

```javascript
const { name: userName } = user;
console.log(userName); // "Ana"
```

You can also provide a default: `const { role = "viewer" } = user;`.
lessons.task: Given `const product = { id: 42, name: "Keyboard", price: 79.99 }`, use destructuring to extract `name` and `price` into variables. Log both.
lessons.hint: Use `const { name, price } = product;` on one line.

lessons.title: Array destructuring and spread
lessons.goal: Unpack array elements into variables and copy an array with spread.
lessons.theory:
Array destructuring unpacks by position:

```javascript
const [first, second, ...rest] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
console.log(first);  // 10
console.log(second); // 20
console.log(rest);   // [30, 40]
```

The **spread operator** `...` expands an array into individual values, useful for copying or combining arrays:

```javascript
const a = [1, 2];
const b = [3, 4];
const combined = [...a, ...b]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]
```
lessons.task: Given `const rgb = [255, 128, 0]`, use array destructuring to get `red`, `green`, and `blue`. Log `red`.
lessons.hint: Square brackets on the left of `=` destructure an array by position.

lessons.title: Methods inside objects
lessons.goal: Add a function as a property of an object and call it.
lessons.task: Create an object `circle` with a property `radius` set to `5` and a method `area()` that returns `Math.PI * this.radius ** 2`. Log `circle.area()`.
lessons.hint: The method uses `this.radius` to read the object's own property. Call it with `circle.area()`.

lessons.title: What the DOM is
lessons.goal: Explain what the DOM is and why JavaScript uses it to change a web page.
lessons.theory:
When the browser loads an HTML file it builds a tree of objects in memory called the **Document Object Model (DOM)**. Every tag in the HTML becomes a **node** in the tree.

JavaScript can read and change that tree at any time. When you change a node, the browser immediately updates the visible page. This is how modern web pages react without reloading.

`document` is the global object that represents the whole page. You use its methods to find nodes and its properties to read page-level information.
lessons.task: Which global object gives you access to the DOM in a browser?
lessons.solution: document
lessons.hint: It is a single lowercase English word that refers to the whole page.

why: Correct: the global `document` object is the entry point to the DOM API.
window.dom does not exist in the browser API.
html is a tag name, not a JavaScript object.
page is not a standard global in browsers.
check.explain: The DOM is accessed through the global `document` object, which represents the loaded HTML page.

lessons.title: querySelector
lessons.goal: Use querySelector to find a single element by CSS selector.
lessons.theory:
`document.querySelector(selector)` returns the **first** element that matches a CSS selector, or `null` if nothing matches:

```javascript
const heading = document.querySelector("h1");
const btn = document.querySelector("#submit");
const card = document.querySelector(".card");
```

- Tag name: `"h1"`
- ID (unique): `"#submit"`
- Class: `".card"`
- You can also use any valid CSS selector: `"nav a.active"`

Always check the result before using it: if the selector matches nothing, the return value is `null` and calling a method on it crashes.
lessons.task: Write a line that selects the element with id `"title"` and stores it in a `const` called `titleEl`.
lessons.solution: const titleEl = document.querySelector("#title");
lessons.hint: Use `"#title"` as the selector. The `#` prefix selects by id.

lessons.title: querySelectorAll
lessons.goal: Use querySelectorAll to get all matching elements and loop over them.
lessons.task: Write a line that selects all elements with class `"card"` and stores them in `const cards`. Then log `cards.length`.
lessons.solution:
const cards = document.querySelectorAll(".card");
console.log(cards.length);
lessons.hint: Use `".card"` (with a dot for class). The length is a property of the NodeList.

lessons.title: Reading element properties
lessons.goal: Read the textContent, id and className of a DOM element.
lessons.theory:
Every DOM element has properties that mirror its HTML attributes and content:

```javascript
const el = document.querySelector("h1");
console.log(el.textContent); // the visible text
console.log(el.id);          // the id attribute
console.log(el.className);   // the class attribute (a string)
```

`textContent` includes the text of all descendant elements. It strips all tags, giving you plain text.

`innerHTML` gives the full HTML markup inside the element. Use it only for reading; writing to `innerHTML` with untrusted data is a security risk (XSS).
lessons.task: What property gives you the plain text content of an element, with all HTML tags stripped?
lessons.solution: textContent
lessons.hint: It is a two-word property joined without a space, describing what kind of content it returns.

why: Correct: textContent returns all text inside the element with HTML tags removed.
innerHTML includes the HTML markup, not just text.
innerText is similar but also reflects CSS styling and can be slower to read.
value is used for form inputs like <input>, not for general elements.
check.explain: textContent gives you the concatenated text of an element and all its descendants, with all HTML tags stripped out.

lessons.title: Changing text and HTML
lessons.goal: Update an element's visible content using textContent and innerHTML.
lessons.task: Write code that selects the element with id `"message"` and sets its `textContent` to `"Updated!"`.
lessons.solution:
const message = document.querySelector("#message");
message.textContent = "Updated!";
lessons.hint: Two lines: one `querySelector`, one assignment to `.textContent`.

lessons.title: Changing inline styles
lessons.goal: Apply CSS properties to an element via its style object.
lessons.task: Select the element with id `"alert"` and set its background color to `"yellow"` and its font size to `"18px"` using the `.style` object.
lessons.hint: `background-color` becomes `.style.backgroundColor` in JavaScript (camelCase).

lessons.title: Adding and removing CSS classes
lessons.goal: Toggle element classes with classList.add, remove, and toggle.
lessons.theory:
The `.classList` property gives you methods to manage classes:

```javascript
const btn = document.querySelector("#btn");
btn.classList.add("active");      // add a class
btn.classList.remove("disabled"); // remove a class
btn.classList.toggle("hidden");   // add if absent, remove if present
btn.classList.contains("active"); // true or false
```

This is the preferred way to change appearance: define states in CSS, then switch classes in JavaScript. It keeps style in CSS and behaviour in JS.
lessons.task: Select `"#nav"` and add the class `"visible"` with `classList.add`. Then use `classList.toggle` to toggle the class `"open"`.
lessons.hint: Three lines: select, add, toggle. Each method call is on the element.

lessons.title: Creating and inserting elements
lessons.goal: Create a new DOM element in JavaScript and append it to the page.
lessons.task:
Create a `

` element, set its `textContent` to `"Hello from JS"`, and append it to the element with id `"container"`.
lessons.hint: Three steps: createElement, set textContent, then appendChild on the parent element.

lessons.title: addEventListener
lessons.goal: Attach an event listener to a DOM element.
lessons.task: Select the element with id `"myBtn"` and add a click listener that logs `"Button clicked"`.
lessons.hint: Two steps: select the button, then call `.addEventListener("click", ...)` on it.

lessons.title: The event object
lessons.goal: Use the event object to read details about what triggered the event.
lessons.task: Add a click listener to `document.querySelector("#box")`. Inside the handler, receive the event as `e` and log `e.target` and `e.type`.
lessons.hint: Name the callback parameter `e` and access its `.target` and `.type` properties.

lessons.title: preventDefault
lessons.goal: Stop the browser's default action for an event.
lessons.task: Add a `"submit"` listener to `document.querySelector("form")`. Inside, call `e.preventDefault()` and log `"form submitted"`.
lessons.hint: The listener goes on the form element with `"submit"` as the event name. `e.preventDefault()` is the first line in the handler.

lessons.title: Event delegation
lessons.goal: Handle events for many child elements by listening on their parent.
lessons.task: What is the main advantage of event delegation over adding a listener to each list item?
lessons.solution: One listener handles all items, including dynamically added ones.
lessons.hint: Think about what happens when you add new items to the list after the page loads.

options: It uses one listener on the parent, which handles all current and future child items.
It is faster because bubbling stops at the first listener it finds.
It only works for click events.
It prevents events from bubbling, so each item stays independent.
why: Correct: a single listener on the parent reacts to events from all descendants, even those added later.
Bubbling does not stop automatically; you have to call stopPropagation for that.
Event delegation works for any bubbling event, not just clicks.
Event delegation relies on bubbling; it does not prevent it.
check.explain: Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent element. Events from children bubble up and are handled there, so the code works for elements added at any time.

lessons.title: What a Promise is
lessons.goal: Describe what a Promise represents and its three states.
lessons.task: A Promise that has finished successfully is in which state?
lessons.solution: fulfilled
lessons.hint: Three states: pending, fulfilled, rejected.

why: Correct: a Promise that finished successfully is in the fulfilled state.
resolved is not an official Promise state, though it is sometimes used loosely.
done is not a Promise state.
completed is not a Promise state.
check.explain: A Promise has three official states: pending (still running), fulfilled (succeeded) and rejected (failed).

lessons.title: fetch: loading data from a URL
lessons.goal: Use fetch to request a URL and chain .then() to handle the response.
lessons.theory:
`fetch(url)` makes an HTTP GET request and returns a Promise that resolves with a **Response** object:

```javascript
fetch("https://api.example.com/users")
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error(error));
```

- `.then(response => response.json())` converts the response body from JSON text to a JavaScript object. This is itself async and returns another Promise.
- The second `.then` receives the parsed data.
- `.catch` handles any network error or JSON parse error.

Chaining `.then` calls is the old way of handling Promises. `async/await` is the modern way.
lessons.task: Write a fetch call to `"https://api.example.com/data"`. Chain a `.then` that calls `response.json()` and a second `.then` that logs `data`. Add a `.catch` that logs the error.
lessons.solution:
fetch("https://api.example.com/data")
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error(error));
lessons.hint: Three chained calls: `.then(response => response.json())`, `.then(data => ...)`, `.catch(error => ...)`.

lessons.title: Checking the response status
lessons.goal: Check whether a fetch response was successful before using its data.
lessons.task: Inside a fetch `.then`, write the guard that throws an Error if `response.ok` is false. The error message should include `response.status`.
lessons.hint: The guard is a single `if` that checks `!response.ok` and throws a new Error.

lessons.title: async functions
lessons.goal: Mark a function async and understand what it always returns.
lessons.task: Write an async function called `fetchMessage` that returns the string `"Hello async"`. (No await needed yet.)
lessons.hint: Just add `async` before `function` and return the string.

lessons.title: await: pause until the Promise settles
lessons.goal: Use await to pause an async function until a Promise resolves.
lessons.task: Write an async function `loadData` that awaits a `fetch` call to `"/api/posts"`, then awaits `response.json()`, and logs the result.
lessons.hint: Two `await` lines inside the function: one for fetch, one for `.json()`.

lessons.title: try/catch with async/await
lessons.goal: Handle errors from await using try/catch.
lessons.task: Wrap the two awaits in `loadData` with a `try/catch`. In the catch block, log the error with `console.error`.
lessons.hint: Everything inside the function goes inside `try {}`. The `catch` block receives an error variable.

lessons.title: Promise.all: run requests in parallel
lessons.goal: Use Promise.all to await multiple Promises at the same time.
lessons.task: Write an async function `loadBoth` that uses `Promise.all` to fetch both `"/api/users"` and `"/api/posts"` in parallel, then logs the two responses.
lessons.hint: Destructure the result of `await Promise.all([...])` into two variables.

lessons.title: Structuring the HTML
lessons.goal: Set up the HTML skeleton for a weather card before writing any JavaScript.
lessons.theory:
Good JavaScript starts with good HTML. For a weather card you need: ```html Weather

–

–

–

``` The script tag is at the **bottom** of the body so the DOM elements exist by the time the JavaScript runs.
lessons.task: Why is the `<script>` tag placed at the bottom of the `<body>` rather than in `<head>`?
lessons.solution: So that all DOM elements exist before the script tries to select them.
lessons.hint: Think about what happens if JavaScript runs before the browser has parsed the HTML elements.

options: So all HTML elements are already in the DOM when the script runs.
So the page loads faster because scripts are bigger than HTML.
Because the browser ignores script tags in the head.
To prevent CSS from overriding JavaScript.
why: Correct: placing the script after the HTML means all elements are available when querySelector runs.
Script placement at the bottom is about DOM availability, not file size.
Browsers do parse and run scripts in the head; they just run before the body elements exist.
CSS and JavaScript do not conflict based on where the script tag is placed.
check.explain: JavaScript that queries the DOM must run after the browser has parsed those elements. Placing the script tag at the end of the body guarantees that.

lessons.title: Selecting all the elements
lessons.goal: Use querySelector to grab every element your script will need.
lessons.task: Write the four `querySelector` lines that select `#city-name`, `#description`, `#temperature`, and `#load-btn` into `cityEl`, `descEl`, `tempEl`, and `loadBtn`.
lessons.hint: Four lines, each `const varName = document.querySelector("#id");`.

lessons.title: Writing the fetch function
lessons.goal: Write an async function that fetches weather data and updates the DOM.
lessons.task: Write an async function `loadWeather` that awaits `fetch("/api/weather")`, throws if `!res.ok`, awaits `res.json()`, and sets `cityEl.textContent` to `data.city`.
lessons.hint: Four lines inside try: await fetch, the guard, await .json(), and the DOM update.

lessons.title: Wiring the button
lessons.goal: Call the async function when the button is clicked.
lessons.theory:
Now connect the button to the function:

```javascript
loadBtn.addEventListener("click", loadWeather);
```

Because `loadWeather` is an async function, calling it returns a Promise. The browser does not do anything with that Promise automatically, so unhandled errors inside `loadWeather` might be silently swallowed. Make sure your `try/catch` is comprehensive.

You could also write it as:

```javascript
loadBtn.addEventListener("click", () => loadWeather());
```

Both are equivalent. The first form is shorter and preferred when the function signatures match.
lessons.task: Add a click listener to `loadBtn` that calls `loadWeather` when clicked.
lessons.starter:
// wire the button
// (assume loadBtn and loadWeather are already defined)
lessons.solution: loadBtn.addEventListener("click", loadWeather);
lessons.hint: Pass `loadWeather` directly as the callback, without calling it immediately.

lessons.title: Disabling the button while loading
lessons.goal: Prevent double submissions by disabling the button during the fetch.
lessons.task: Set `loadBtn.disabled = true` at the start of `loadWeather` and re-enable it in a `finally` block.
lessons.hint: One line before `try` sets disabled to true. A `finally` block after `catch` sets it back to false.

lessons.title: Showing a loading state
lessons.goal: Update the DOM to show loading text while the fetch runs.
lessons.task: Before the `try` block in `loadWeather`, set `cityEl.textContent` to `"Loading..."` and `loadBtn.disabled` to `true`.
lessons.hint: Add `cityEl.textContent = "Loading...";` on a new first line inside `loadWeather`, before the existing `loadBtn.disabled` line.

lessons.title: Rendering a list from an array
lessons.goal: Take an array from the API and build a list of DOM elements from it.
lessons.task: Given `const list = document.querySelector("#list")` and `const items = ["Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"]`, clear the list and append one `<li>` per item.
lessons.hint: Clear with `list.innerHTML = ""`. Then forEach: createElement, set textContent, appendChild.

lessons.title: Putting it all together
lessons.goal: Describe the complete flow of a JavaScript mini project from button click to DOM update.
lessons.theory:
A complete interactive page follows this flow:

1. The browser parses HTML and builds the DOM.
2. The script tag at the bottom loads and runs.
3. `querySelector` grabs the elements the script needs.
4. An event listener is attached to the button.
5. The user clicks the button.
6. The listener calls the async fetch function.
7. The function sets a loading state and disables the button.
8. `fetch` sends the HTTP request and awaits the response.
9. The response is checked and parsed.
10. The DOM elements are updated with the data.
11. The button is re-enabled in `finally`.

This pattern repeats in every web application. The names change, the shape stays the same.
lessons.task: In which step does the user first see a change in the page after clicking the button?
lessons.solution: When the loading state is set, immediately on click.
lessons.hint: The fetch has not even started yet at that point.

options: When the loading state text is set, immediately after the click.
When the fetch request is sent to the server.
When the server sends back its response.
When response.json() finishes parsing the body.
why: Correct: setting textContent to "Loading..." is synchronous and updates the DOM right away, before the fetch even starts.
Sending the request is async and the user sees no visual change from it.
The response arrives over the network, long after the first visual update.
Parsing the JSON is also async and happens after the network round-trip.
check.explain: The first visible change is the loading text set synchronously before the first await. The DOM updates immediately without waiting for the network.
